newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kinshasa business prepares for Zaire rebel siege.
newsitem.headline: Kinshasa business prepares for Zaire rebel siege.

text.p: The business community in Zaire's capital Kinshasa made preparations on Sunday in case a rapid rebel advance cut the city's main supply route.
Bankers said importers were looking at shifting supplies from Zaire's Atlantic port of Matadi to neighbouring Congo.
"At least one shipper is already doing it and others are considering doing so as well," said a Western banker.

The business community appeared to be reacting to the announcement on Saturday by rebel leader Laurent Kabila that he had recruited 100,000 new guerrillas and was ready to open another front for a final push to dislodge President Mobutu Sese Seko.
"It won't take long. We'll be in Kinshasa very soon. We're only 200 km (120 miles) away from Kinshasa," Kabila said in Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi, seized by his rebels just over a week ago.
His comments at a rally seemed to confirm widespread rumours in Kinshasa that rebel forces were grouping in western Zaire to cut off the capital from its only access to the sea.
Lebanese traders in Kinshasa, who dominate the retail trade, said they had bought extra stock in the last few weeks in case supplies were cut or the city suffered a long siege.
The stock was stored in high-security warehouses to protect it against looting from Zaire's underpaid army, which has regularly run amok before fleeing the rebel advance.
The vast Central African state's only seaport is at Matadi on the small Atlantic coastline. It is the site of the country's lifeblood oil refinery and the gateway for most imported goods.

Kabila's announcement, even if exaggerated in terms of the number of recruits, looked certain to put more pressure on the ailing Mobutu, who grudgingly agreed to meet the guerrilla leader in a desperate bid to negotiate an end to the spreading civil war.
Kinshasa is the last stronghold of Mobutu and his ragged government army. The rebels now control about half the country and look set to end his 32-year rule.
His government is trying to use what little diplomatic clout it has left to force a ceasefire on the rebels.
Benin President Mathieu Kerekou was due in Kinshasa to meet Mobutu on Sunday but the visit was cancelled at the last minute without explanation.
South Africa last week finally persuaded Mobutu to meet Kabila for the direct negotiations the rebel leader has long demanded as a way of ending the war.
But diplomats are sceptical about Kabila's interest in reaching any compromise given his overwhelming military advantage on the ground.

Western Zaire borders Angola, whose government has been cited in recent Belgian press reports as backing Kabila, apparently in revenge for Mobutu's support of Angolan UNITA rebels during the southern African nation's own civil war.
Aid workers on Sunday accused Zairean rebels of playing games with the lives of Rwandan refugees and said many faced death because of delays in their repatriation.

About 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees have been living in appalling conditions at Biaro and Kasese camps south of Kisangani since rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo/Zaire captured the city on March 15.

In Beirut, a Lebanese official said the rebels had agreed to release 46 Lebanese nationals held as hostages under a deal brokered by Lebanese residents with Beirut's embassies in Zaire and South Africa.
